raw_text:
### Introduction & Epidemiology

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic, potentially life-threatening form of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction that occurs during the last month of pregnancy or within the first few postpartum months in women without previous heart disease [1,2]. The clinical diagnosis of exclusion relies on demonstrating a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) typically below 45% [2,3]. While rare globally, PPCM exhibits marked geographic variation, with a disproportionately high incidence in regions like Haiti and South Africa [3,4]. Recognized risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestations, black ancestry, chronic hypertension, and preeclampsia [4,5].

### Pathophysiology

The molecular etiology of PPCM was long considered elusive, but a "two-hit" model integrating vascular and genetic vulnerability has recently emerged [6,7]. A pivotal mechanism involves the systemic oxidative stress-induced cleavage of the hormone prolactin [6]. In this pathway, elevated cathepsin D levels cleave full-length 23-kDa prolactin into an angiostatic and pro-apoptotic 16-kDa fragment [6]. This toxic isoform damages capillary networks, promotes endothelial apoptosis, and disrupts cardiomyocyte metabolism [6]. Simultaneously, late-pregnancy angiogenic imbalance—characterized by high secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) from the placenta—exacerbates endothelial dysfunction by neutralizing vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) [7].

Furthermore, research has highlighted a strong genetic predisposition to PPCM, demonstrating overlapping genetic architecture with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) [8,9]. Notably, loss-of-function variants in the titin gene (*TTN*), which encodes the giant sarcomeric protein titin, are identified in up to 15% of PPCM patients [9,10]. Other genetic mutations implicate proteins involved in desmosomal structure and calcium handling [11,12]. This genetic susceptibility likely renders the maternal heart unable to cope with the profound hemodynamic stressors of pregnancy and the postpartum period [11,12].

### Clinical Presentation & Diagnosis

PPCM commonly presents with signs and symptoms of acute heart failure, such as dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, and peripheral edema [13,14]. Because these symptoms overlap with normal physiological changes of late pregnancy and the early puerperium, delays in diagnosis are frequent and can result in severe adverse outcomes, including cardiogenic shock and thromboembolism [13,15]. Standard diagnostic workup requires transthoracic echocardiography to document left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF <45%) and exclude other causes of heart failure [15,16]. Cardiac biomarkers like N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and troponins are highly valuable for risk stratification and monitoring treatment response [16,17].

### Management

Therapeutic strategies must be tailored to the maternal-fetal state [18,19]. During pregnancy, standard heart failure regimens must avoid teratogenic agents such as angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) [18,19]. Safe alternatives include hydralazine/nitrates and beta-blockers (preferably beta-1 selective agents like metoprolol) [19]. Postpartum, treatment can be optimized to include ACE inhibitors/ARBs, MRAs, and sacubitril/valsartan if breastfeeding is avoided [19,20].

A major breakthrough in PPCM-specific therapy is the use of bromocriptine, a dopamine D2-receptor agonist that inhibits prolactin secretion [20,21]. Clinical trials, particularly in Germany and South Africa, have demonstrated that adding bromocriptine to standard heart failure therapy improves LVEF recovery and clinical outcomes [21,22]. Due to the pro-thrombotic properties of bromocriptine and the postpartum state, concomitant anticoagulation (with heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin) is mandatory [21,23]. Advanced mechanical circulatory support, such as extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) or left ventricular assist devices (LVADs), serves as a crucial bridge to recovery or transplantation in refractory cases [18,24].

### Prognosis & Future Pregnancies

The prognosis of PPCM has dramatically improved with contemporary guideline-directed medical therapy, with LVEF recovery rates ranging from 50% to 70% within six months of diagnosis [15,25]. However, the risk of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies remains a critical concern [25,26]. Women with persistent left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF <50%–55%) face a high risk of clinical deterioration, heart failure relapse, and maternal mortality in subsequent gestations [27,28]. Consequently, pregnancy is strongly discouraged in this subgroup [27,29]. Even in women with fully recovered LVEF, there remains a 20% to 30% risk of relapse, demanding extensive preconception counseling and close multidisciplinary monitoring throughout any subsequent pregnancy [28,30].
